DISASTROUS FIRE IN BUSINESS SECTION
subsubtopic: CO-OPERATION OF OTHER AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege, and if I take longer than usual in stating my question I would ask your indulgence, sir.
I should like to tell the house very briefly a story of co-operation and courage that keeps alive one's faith in human nature.
Last Saturday at midnight a fire broke out in Brockville which at one time threatened the entire business section of the town, but, through superhuman effort, was confined to one city block. In spite of the heroic efforts of the Brockville Are department it was soon found that to control the fire was beyond the power of one department; therefore urgent appeals were made to other centres, whose response was immediate.
The first to arrive were the fire fighters from the Royal Canadian Regiment with army equipment. Almost immediately firemen and fire trucks from Prescott, Athens and Smiths Falls were on the scene, and, as soon as they could be ferried across the St. Lawrence river, a pumper, aerial ladder truck, crew and special police force from Ogdensburg, New York, arrived. Seamen from the Canadian navy sloop Oriol, which happened to be in port, joined forces with the firemen, soldiers and citizens, so the fire was ultimately brought under control by complete municipal and military aid and international co-operation.
Fire fighting is always hazardous, but with the temperature at almost zero it becomes an almost unbearable ordeal. Throughout the night a group of young women kept the fire fighters supplied with hot coffee and sandwiches, while others were on hand to crack ice off the fire fighters' coats, helmets, gloves and boots.
Fortunately no lives were lost and no serious injuries suffered, but nearly one hundred persons were made homeless.
On Sunday morning appeals for assistance were made from all the pulpits of the Brockville churches, and at one o'clock Mayor W. Fred Reynolds spoke over radio station CFJM to ask for money, clothing and other
necessities. By five o'clock on Sunday afternoon the receiving centre had been moved no less than three times in order to provide greater accommodation for the mass of goods that started to pour in, and by nine in the evening half the second floor of the city hall looked like a department store. In addition, the sum of $2,500 had been received in cash donations, and I am told the fund is now over $6,000. One farmer arrived with two dozen eggs, and emptied his purse, which contained $1.03. An elderly woman donated $1.85, and said that it was all she had at the moment, but that she would give more on Wednesday when her pay cheque arrived.
The generosity of the people of Brockville exceeds the bounds of any possible expectation; and what applies to Brockville extends to the entire district, which includes several communities in northern New York state. Truly the cardinal Christian principle, "love thy neighbour" knows no international boundary in North America.
A disaster such as Brockville has just experienced brings out, in no uncertain way, the best in all of us, regardless of race or creed, and serves to make us proud that we are Canadians and fortunate enough to live on the continent of North America.
I should like to thank the Prime Minister, the Acting Minister of National Defence, and the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence for the prompt and sympathetic attention given the request that certain huts at the Royal Canadian Regiment camp be made available to the municipal authorities at Brockville. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that these huts will serve a most useful and humane purpose in looking after the temporary housing needs of the hundred men, women and children who were made homeless as a result of the worst fire in the history of Brockville.

PRESS REPORT OF REMARKS OF MR. JONES IN DEBATE ON NOVEMBER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in yesterday's Ottawa Citizen there is a report of a statement made by the general manager of the Ottawa board of trade which refers to my speech on the bill to establish a national trade mark. I am charged with being unfair to Ottawa merchants. The article states that I implied that there was a general practice among Ottawa merchants of misleading the public by using well-known containers to hold inferior products. Such a statement is incorrect.
I mentioned that stores on Elgin street used containers bearing the "O.K. brand" label to hold a local product of inferior quality. My contention is that a container bearing the name of a well-known brand should not be used for any other product. Even today those containers are still on display, filled with other than Okanagan produce. The article in question makes the statement that I said merchants filled containers with these products, and marked them as coming from the Okanagan valley. What I did say was that Okanagan valley containers were refilled with other, and in the case under review, inferior, quality produce. I shall be pleased to supply Mr. Cairns with the evidence if he so desires.
The other point with which I wish to deal is the charge that I was derelict in my duty in not bringing this matter to the attention of the house earlier in the session. May I point out that a perusal of Hansard will show that I dealt with this matter earlier in the session, but so far no action has been taken. I did not at any time, nor do I now, suggest that the practice is general among Ottawa merchants.
May I repeat that the principle involved in my speech is that containers marked with a well-known brand name should not be used again, once the original contents which fulfilled the specifications of that brand have been emptied out.

I should like to put myself on record as supporting the point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I do not think this matter should be dealt with with the hilarity and lightness that is displayed by hon. gentlemen on the other side

of the house. It took us a long time to get a fair wage clause in government contracts. We should like the fair wage clause in government contracts to apply to all contracts. I do not know whether I am right or not, but my understanding is that the fair wage clause applies to all federal government contracts, or to any federal government assisted contract. If that is so, it should apply in this instance. If it does not apply to a contract in which the federal government assists, it should apply, because the federal government should not supply money that is to be used in construction or manufacturing where unfair working and wage conditions prevail. We should make it clear that when the federal government assists any project it does so on the understanding that fair wages and fair working conditions apply. These conditions are not particularly onerous, because they are the conditions that apply in the locality. They are not conditions arbitrarily imposed. There is a formula for working them out.
I suggest that hon. members on the opposite side, who appeal to workers for support at election time, take this matter seriously and see that these fair wage clauses are in the contracts.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, just to keep the record straight may I say this? The hon. member for Vancouver East said that it took a long time to establish the principle of fair wages and working conditions. Let me say to him that that took place before his time and mine. I think it was in the year 1900. The political party that laid down that principle was the Liberal party. My hon. friend knows that the wage structure across the nation is not the same in every province. In British Columbia they have a comparatively high wage structure, probably the highest in the dominion. I think people engaged in public works in that province would wish to see the prevailing conditions in Vancouver or in British Columbia generally adhered to. I feel certain that if we had a national approach to the problem we would object to the wage structures in some of the other provinces. My hon. friend can rest assured that the provincial people, who have jurisdiction in this matter will see to it that the legislation and regulations affecting fair wage conditions in effect in their respective provinces are adhered to.

speechtext:
I cannot agree with the minister when he says the Liberal government was the first government to recognize the principle of fair wage contracts in agreements. That is true in theory, but it was not until the war contracts of 1939 and 1940 were let that the government gave effect to the fair wage conditions so far as federal government

contracts were concerned. As the hon. member for Vancouver East pointed out a moment ago, some of us in the house were fighting for these things thirty years ago. It is true that we recognized the principle, but it was never put into effect. Unless we are prepared to follow out the mechanics laid down by the government in federal contracts during the war, we shall slowly get back to where we were when the matter was just a theory. It was put in the contracts during the war.
We are not asking that any of the wage schedules in the provinces be upset. All we are asking is that when the federal government lets a contract, the contractor be obliged to conform to the wages and conditions established by the provinces. It must be remembered that conditions are not the same from section to section in a province. There is a differential. If a contractor is putting the highway through a certain section of the province, and the provincial government has set out a fair wage schedule, the least the contractor should be obliged to do is to conform to the law applicable in that particular section.
The minister knows well that since the war there has been difficulty with federal contracts. I brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of Transport since the present session in regard to federal works projects in my own community, where there was no difficulty during the war, although a lot of construction work was carried on. The contractor got out from under, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggested, by saying that the provincial laws had nothing to do with it; that it was a federal contract. The Minister of Transport in this case stated clearly that once that contract is let, it is the responsibility of the contractors to establish the wages and conditions they see fit. A clause should be written into the contract providing that the contractor, in matters of labour, employment and wages should conform to the standards set up in that particular part of the country. Nothing would be upset at all; it would be simply writing something into the contract to avoid difficulties in the future.
I know that in the letting of federal contracts early in the war there was a complete upset right across the country. In my own section of Canada one of my main jobs was running from one works project to another in an effort to iron out difficulties with truck drivers and labourers as between federal contracts and provincial laws, and all that kind of thing. We do not want to get back to that. We are merely asking that the practical machinery established during the war-because once it was established it worked well-be used. These contracts are
Trans-Canada Highway not yet let. It is not necessary to have a special provision in the bill. But if the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply and the Minister of Labour could get together and have a little talk I am sure there would be no trouble in writing into the contracts a clause in which it would be asked that contractors conform to provincial laws in this regard.

We should have some understanding of the method of determining the amount of contribution. If the total amount is limited to $150 million for seven years, it means a little more than $20 million a year. There are ten provinces. With the federal contribution of fifty per cent, this allows for a yearly average of construction of roughly $40 million. Again on a straight numerical basis this is an average of about $4 million per year per province.
We know the difficulties of construction in some parts of Ontario, for instance, and British Columbia. It is possible that merely in carrying out their own highway program a province might wish to do more than $4 million worth of construction in any year. What is to be the position? Is there to be a limit placed on the construction that any one province may carry out in any one year? How is the apportionment among provinces to be made? Suppose one province, with this in mind, does a lot of construction early-let us say $20 million or $30 million in a year; then are not the other provinces in danger of having less of the share of the $150 million, if they do not get in at the start? Will that not be the position, unless they know there will be a basis of apportionment, and what that basis is to be? What has the minister in mind in that respect?

speechtext: The money will be spent as the work is done. There will be no attempt to allot on an annual basis, or break it down by provinces in relation to the expenditures that we think should be incurred. Nor will there be any attempt to spread out the $150 million over seven years. The seven-year period provision was put in there largely at the request of certain provinces which felt that, having regard to their present heavy highways program, they could not take on the additional work of the trans-Canada highway and complete it in a shorter period of time. The federal government is prepared to go ahead as quickly as the provinces wish to do so, and the expenditures will be in direct relationship to the mileage of work completed.

I think section 4 is the most important one in the bill. It is the section concerning which a great deal of the discussion has already taken place. It is the provision whereby the federal government's contribution to the building of the trans-Canada highway will amount to no more than fifty per cent. I was particularly glad to see the stand taken by the leader of the opposition and the leader of the Social Credit party when they pointed out that a fifty per cent contribution is too low to assure the building of a trans-Canada highway within the seven-year period. If the highway is to be built within a reasonable time, the contribution of fifty per cent should be increased, so that there will be a greater incentive for each province to undertake construction within its own boundaries. The minister has said the building of the trans-Canada highway is contingent upon all provinces signing agreements. With a contribution of only fifty per cent I would say that the cost may be too high for some provinces to proceed.
I was greatly impressed by the speech of the leader of the Social Credit party. He pointed out that even for a province as wealthy as Alberta the contribution required from the province for the building of the highway within its boundaries will be a serious burden on the provincial treasury. If this is so in Alberta, certainly some of the maritime provinces, and likely the province of Saskatchewan, will have even greater difficulty in attempting to match the federal contribution dollar for dollar. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the fifty per cent contribution be increased to seventy-five per cent. If the federal government's contribution is increased, I believe that each province will be able to go ahead with the construction of a trans-Canada highway in the near future.
Trans-Canada Highway
I should like, therefore, to move an amendment, Mr. Chairman, seconded by the member for Saskatoon. The amendment is as follows:
That clause 4, subclause (2), be amended by deleting therefrom the words "fifty per centum" and by substituting therefor the words "seventy-five per centum."
This amendment will in no way increase the expenditure made by the federal government under this act. The expenditure to be made under this act is covered by clause 7, which states that the aggregate of all expenditures shall not exceed $150 million. All this amendment would do is to change the formula, so that the provinces could undertake construction. I admit that it might mean a reduction in the standard of the highway; I do not know. It would at least assure the building of a trans-Canada highway, and it would establish the principle that the federal government should make a greater contribution.
The federal government has found that in many cases, such as old age pensions and housing, it must make a seventy-five per cent contribution to enable the provinces to fulfil their obligation. The same principle should be applied to the building of the trans-Canada highway. If the government really desires the highway it should be prepared to pay seventy-five per cent of the cost, while the provinces contribute twenty-five per cent.

I ask you, sir, and members opposite to take their time in considering this matter. It is quite clear that the amendment is in order. May I remind you, sir, and all hon. members, of the statement my colleague the member for Assiniboia has just made, namely, that clause 7 of the bill sets a ceiling on the amount of money to be spent under this bill. If the bill is passed without this amendment, the total amount of money to be spent will be $150 million. If my colleague's amendment carries and the bill passes with the "seventy-five per centum" in clause 4, the total amount of money to be spent by this government will still be only $150 million. All this amendment does is to relax the terms upon which the federal government is making the money available.
If I may illustrate by using a figure, in order for a province to secure $3 of federal money now, it has to match it with another $3.

Trans-Canada Highway [f my colleague's amendment carries, in order for a province to get $3 of federal money, it would have to match it with only $1. As my colleague has stated, it might result in less money being spent on the highway, but at least it would make it possible for the highway to be started, and it would establish the principle of a three to one contribution.
On Saturday last the member for Rimouski, who is parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, introduced a bill to amend the Industrial Development Bank Act. The amending bill was introduced without any prior resolution. In introducing it, the parliamentary assistant explained why there was no prior resolution. He said that it was not a money bill-that is did not involve expenditure. The member for Coast-Capilano is now nodding his head up and down. The member for Rimouski said that the Industrial Development Bank Act sets a ceiling of $25 million. All that his amendment did was to relax the terms on which a portion of that money is to be made available. He said that because it did not change the ceiling of $25 million, it did not involve an increase in expenditure. Mr. Chairman, the cases are completely analogous.
The bill before us sets a ceiling of $150 million, and the purpose of my colleague's amendment is to relax the terms on which that federal money is to be made available to the provinces. I submit that members opposite cannot claim one rule for the government on Saturday, and apply another rule to the opposition on Tuesday. If on Saturday it was in order for the member for Rimouski to say that his amendment did not involve an increase in expenditure, because it left the ceiling where it was and merely relaxed the terms on which that money was made available, I submit it is in order today for the member for Assiniboia to move an amendment that leaves the ceiling at $150 million, and merely relaxes the terms on which that money is to be made available.
I could go further, Mr. Chairman, and read from pages 510 and 511 of May, but I will simply paraphrase it. On those pages it says that once the resolution preceding a bill has been brought in with the royal recommendation, no amendments can be made that go beyond the terms of the resolution; in other words no amendment can exceed the scope of the royal recommendation. May I remind you, sir, that when the minister of reconstruction brought in the resolution preceding this bill, it did not specify any plan of contribution. There was no mention of a fifty-fifty basis. The rule is quite clear that when the house is in committee on a bill, any

amendment to the terms of the bill can be made, provided it does not go beyond the terms laid down in the resolution which was laid before the house with the royal recommendation.
I turn to the resolution, which is on page 2023 of Hansard. It reads:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to encourage and assist in the construction of a trans-Canada highway and to provide for this purpose that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply may enter into agreements with any provinces providing for the payment by Canada to those provinces of contributions in respect of the cost of a trans-Canada highway; with provision also for the employment of temporary engineers, technical officers and other employees for the purpose of the act.
The proposal to which the governor general gave his approval-that is what counts in these matters-was a plan which involved contributions couched in general terms. When the royal recommendation was received, the resolution did not mention a fifty-fifty basis, or any other specific plan. So long as we stay within the terms of the resolution, we are in order, and that is precisely what this amendment does.
But I come back to what I said before, Mr. Chairman, that not only are we staying strictly within the terms of the resolution but we are at this point moving an amendment that does not involve an increased expenditure of money, any more than the amending bill did which the hon. member for Rimouski brought in on Saturday last. I submit that if the rule applies one way for the government on Saturday, it should apply in the same way for the opposition on Tuesday.

The provinces will put up fifty per cent of the cost, which will mean another $150 million coming from the provinces. I see a difficulty in that.
Supposing the provinces have already made plans for a highway program to cover the next two or three years. I believe some of the provincial governments look several years ahead, and plan accordingly. I shall give you an example of what I have in mind. Suppose when construction of the trans-Canada highway commences a province has decided to spend $10 million on its over-all highway program; so much is allotted to first-class, hard-surfaced highways; so much for second-class gravelled highways, and so much for third-class or market roads which are only
Trans-Canada Highway graded. This program calls for an expenditure of $10 million for that year. The dominion government then says it proposes to spend $5 million in that province on the trans-Canada highway in that year. The provincial government may say that will mean we shall have to get another $5 million from some place. We have already planned a $10 million program, so where are we going to get this $5 million. We cannot raise that much. Has the government anticipated a situation of that kind? What will they propose if that happens?
I am afraid that in such a situation the province may say, "We will have to cut our program in half and take $5 million from what we proposed to spend in some other part of the province, and put it on the trans-Canada highway so that we can get $5 million from the federal government this year". I rather favoured the amendment that was proposed by the member for Assiniboia, because if the provinces are to put up fifty per cent, will it not mean that they will have to depreciate part of their over-all program for municipal and secondary roads which are needed. In some cases, perhaps the provincial population needs those roads more than the trans-Canada highway. I know what happens in some of these provinces, because I live in one of them. Alberta has some good hard-surfaced roads, which were built in the hope of encouraging the tourist trade. We will not criticize that. There are some people, however, who do not live near those highways and they say, "What about us?" Those people live there all the time, and have to take their stock or grain to market. The tourist does not live in that province. Whether or not the criticism is justified, I am unable to say; but if any province, because of lack of funds, has to divert funds from its highway program in order to back the dominion government in building the trans-Canada highway, then there may be trouble brewing from certain sections of the public.
I should like to know whether the minister has anticipated any such thing, and how that situation will be met. I know the minister can say he has confidence in the provinces; he has always received co-operation from them and does not expect such a situation to arise. I should like some expression from the minister about that.

Why the necessity for the words in the last part of subsection 2 which read as follows: " ... as determined by the governor in council?" The hon. member for Vancouver -Quadra asked a question about this and I am uneasy over the minister's answer. The subsection reads in full as follows:
The contributions paid to a province under this section shall not exceed1 fifty per centum of the cost to the province of the construction of the highway as determined by the governor in council.
I can see no reason for these words, because section 3 of the bill clearly lays down the procedure which will be followed in determining the cost of the construction, and that cost has to be determined in accordance with the agreement arrived at between the dominion and the respective provinces. The agreements provide for, among other things, the right of the minister to inspect the tenders for the construction of the road; the right of the minister to inspect the road while it is being constructed; the method of determining the cost of construction; the amount of the contributions and the examination, inspection and audit of all construction costs and accounts. Therefore the method of determining the costs of construction is covered in the agreement. In addition, the minister has the right to inspect the work while it is in progress to make sure that it is being carried out

efficiently, and to examine all contracts, and so on, and make certain that there is no room for overexpenditure or careless expenditure.
In view of that clear right of supervision which is given, and the provision for determining the costs of construction in the agreement, it seems to me that it would be quite unfair and unnecessary to give the overriding power to the governor in council under section 4 to determine what is the actual cost of construction. I would be inclined to recommend that the words should be taken out of the bill, but before doing so I would be much obliged to the minister if he would let us know why he considers these words must be in the bill.

Mr. Chairman, could we not get back from British Columbia to the House of Commons in committee considering this bill? The purpose of the bill is to provide half the cost of a transcontinental highway. There are some provinces where there are portions of roads that may be used as a part of the transcontinental highway. It is intended that, with respect to those portions, their value as a part of the transcontinental highway will be taken into account so that the provinces may be reimbursed for a portion of what is already in existence, but not exceeding fifty per cent of its cost. There are some portions of road in the province of Quebec that may be a part of the transcontinental highway, and which are already hard surfaced. I do not think they would be up to the specifications required for the transcontinental highway. It may be that they will be worth a certain portion of what it would cost if there were nothing there, but it is only that portion that will be taken into account, and all that will be a part of the agreement with the province.
The province will determine where the highway is to go. Engineers will then determine how much has been done that is of value as a part of the highway and is up to the specifications required by the contract. For that value the governor in council will determine certain reimbursement to the provinces not exceeding fifty per cent of what it originally cost in any event. That is the scheme, and all this is to be a part of agreements with the provinces. We do not want to step into their field and tell them what they shall do or where they shall do it, but we say: If you want us to contribute to it as something that will be of national value, you have got to build it to a certain standard. If you like you can make it better than that standard, but you have got to build it to a certain standard, and it is only the portion of the cost up to that standard towards which we will make a contribution.
I do not believe we can have any estimate at this time, because a moment ago the hon. member listened to two of my good friends
2410

Trans-Canada Highway from the province of Quebec. One of them wanted the highway to be built on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, and the other wanted it to be built on the north shore of the St. Lawrence. There are some roads there which would be of some use as part of a transcontinental highway, but they were not built at the same time. The widths are not the same, and the curves are not the same. Many of the portions over which I have travelled would have to be improved to bring them up to the standard that will be required in our trans-Canada highway.
Until there has been a determination of where it will be, and an examination by provincial and federal engineers to determine the worth of existing portions of the road, or what it might cost to make a new road, we cannot have any estimate of how much will be spent in that way. In any event, it cannot be more than half the original cost. That clause was put in because it was felt it should not be more than the cost, and costs are apt to be higher today than they were when some of these portions of the road were built. We put that in as the ceiling, and the rest is to be determined after investigation by the engineers of its worth as an element in the national highway.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
There is a question or two I should like to have cleared up. When discussing this matter in the house the other day, or even prior to that, I had occasion to ask the minister some questions regarding it. These questions were answered by a return which may be found in Votes and Proceedings, No. 14. Among the questions asked was this one:
Under the National Housing Act integrated housing scheme is there a regulation covering a 25 per cent holdback of the proceeds of a joint loan to the builder building for sale?
The answer was a very decided no. The answer reads as follows:
No. However, under the 1949 integrated plan the builder is required to transfer title to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at the floor joist
National Housing Act
stage of construction and is required to trustee with the corporation the purchaser's deposit or down payment. When the property is completed and the builder has executed a transfer of title to the purchaser the conveyance to the corporation is then cancelled and the purchaser's down payment is paid over to the builder. Prior to release of the trusteed deposit to the builder steps are taken to ensure that he has paid all carrying charges on the property up to date of completion, including interest on advances made under the mortgage loan, taxes and fire insurance premium; otherwise the equivalent of such carrying charges are deducted from the trusteed deposit.
The point that I wish to make is this. The minister stated definitely that there was no regulation regarding the 25 per cent deposit. That is borne out to a degree by the pamphlet which was issued by the integrated housing plan. My mind goes back, Mr. Chairman, to the bill that we passed the other day on Canadian trade-marks. This integrated housing plan of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation appears to me to be somewhat similar to a Canadian trade-mark. Therefore when people see this pamphlet issued by a government corporation they should be able to put some reliance in it, just as they can rely on goods which have been processed and which have a Canadian trademark upon them.
When I look at this pamphlet I find it says: "The integrated housing plan". The pages are not numbered, therefore I cannot give a page number; but the heading says: "Release of the customary builder's holdback". Let me just mention that for a moment, Mr. Chairman. Without doubt anyone would think that there was a holdback; otherwise why the heading? The following paragraph says:
In the case of loans made under the integrated housing plan, there is no sales' holdback. However, a sum equal to the amount specified in the Mechanics' Lien Act of the province in which the project is built is generally retained until thirty-one days after the completion of the unit.
I do not know whether the minister misunderstood whait I intended when I asked the question. I asked him:
Under the National Housing Act integrated housing scheme is there a regulation covering a 25 per cent holdback of the proceeds of a joint loan to the builder building for sale?
He might have taken that to mean at this moment, and he said "No", which would be in accordance with this little pamphlet I quoted from. According to the pamphlet it would be correct, but according to the title it would be wrong. The hon. member for Battle River asks me what the name of the pamphlet is. It is called:	"The Integrated
Housing Plan." It is published by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, Ottawa, Canada, and the marks on it are RCM-3. The heading of the paragraph to which I referred

National Housing Act
reads:	"Release of the customary builder's holdback". My question to the minister is: Was there a regulation governing that holdback? I am putting it in the past tense now.

speechtext: I am qualifying it. I am speaking from memory now. I do not recall any holdback.

The minister has his
officials in front of him. I want to get the point definitely established because there is a contradiction. I want to know whether there was a regulation governing that 25 per cent holdback. The minister ought to be able to ascertain definitely that there was not.

speechtext:
I mentioned the trade-mark in which the people of Canada place their faith. I hold in my hand a pamphlet issued by a government corporation, and it gives certain information. That information is given to the prospective purchasers. Surely they ought to be able to put some reliance in the statements issued by the government. The minister says "No".
Let me read from another pamphlet. The hon. member for Battle River asks me what the name of this one is. Do not let me confuse you: the name of this one is exactly the same as the other one. It is called "The Integrated Housing Plan, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation." This is published by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, Ottawa, Canada-RCM-3. It is exactly the same book, except that this one was issued when this housing project, particularly the one in Calgary, was under construction, and at a time when a great many other projects throughout the country were under construction.
The other one is a recent publication. Let me read from this one-and, incidentally, it has the stamp on it of the parliamentary library. That was the only place I could get it. I sent to Central Mortgage and Housing for the other one, and got it; but that was not the one with which I was concerned.
Now I turn to article 7, which deals with the same thing, and I read this heading: "Release of the customary builder's holdback". It is exactly the same heading as appears in the other pamphlet. But listen to what I read now:
Under the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation regulations-

Under the regulations, mind you-
-a proportion of the proceeds of a joint loan to a builder building for sale is withheld until the house has been sold to a satisfactory purchaser. In the case of loans made under the integrated housing plan, the holdback is released on completion of the unit.
Now, I ask the minister again: Is there a regulation covering that?

speechtext:

It was at that point I asked the minister if there was a holdback, or a regulation covering holdback. He told me at that time there was not. Then I took another booklet, just exactly the same heading, and issued by the same corporation. And under the same paragraph 7 the heading starts out in exactly the same way,-"Release of the customary builder's holdback". But in the paragraph following that it states definitely-well, just let me read it again so that there will be no misunderstanding-
Under the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation regulations, a proportion of the proceeds of a joint loan to a builder building for sale is withheld until the house has been sold to a satisfactory purchaser. subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Well then, can the minister tell us this:	Why is this governmentauthorized pamphlet, issued by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, given out to the public? When they buy a house they see there is a regulation holding back 25 per cent for their safety. Then the government tell us there is no such regulation. What are the public going to expect? What can they expect? What security have they, when they rely upon a statement of the government, for their protection, when they buy these houses? They assume they have behind them a reliable

241S
organization, such as the government. Then they find they are fleeced out of every cent they have got. When they try to get restitution the government says, "That's just your tough luck. There was no regulation. Although we said there was, that was just to kid you. Now there is none."
This is an exceedingly serious situation. The other day we passed legislation to place a Canadian trade-mark on goods processed in this country, so that when the people of Canada see that government stamp on it they will know they are getting something worth while. Yet, here the government put out a publication, with their stamp on it, and it does not mean a thing. In fact, it is a lie, which has been admitted by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS

Mr. Chairman, I have no desire at all to hold up the bill. I do wish to get the information, however, because it is exceedingly important, so far as I am
National Housing Act
concerned. I am not asking the questions out of idleness, nor do I ask them to embarrass the minister. I have a very definite purpose in mind. Perhaps I need not go further than that in my explanation. I have completed that part with respect to the leaflets.

speechtext: Progress?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
It is progress in the construction of houses, in the long run, I hope. The other question I want to ask arises out of a series of questions I asked some time ago. The first question and answer were as follows:
Under the N.H.A. integrated housing scheme is there an inspection and/or an appraisal fee of $20 permitted?
Yes.
The next question and answer were as follows:
If so, what work is to be performed in order to earn this fee?
When completing an application for a National Housing Act loan the applicant agrees to pay an appraisal fee of $20 for which the lending institution makes an inspection of the site and completes an appraisal of the proposed property. The lending institution inspects the property at various stages of construction to assure that standards under the National Housing Act and the plans and specifications are being substantially followed and to determine the extent to which mortgage moneys may be advanced to the borrower.
My other questions were as follows:
If so, what work is to be performed in order to earn this fee?
Must this $20 fee apply to each individual's property?
Must there be a properly written inspection and/or appraisal form made for each individual's property before this fee is chargeable?
To whom is the fee payable?
If the work is performed for the $20, I have no kick, but in many cases the work is not performed and that is why I am objecting. I am not going to hesitate to name the mortgage company I have in mind because I do not want it to become confused with others which are performing what I would call a legitimate service. The Manufacturers Life has received these $20 payments and they have not raised a finger as far as inspection is concerned because there is not yet a board laid on the lots. However, they have

National Housing Act
charged $20 as an inspection fee. They have a number of houses to build and the fee of $20 is charged in every case, whether there has been construction or not. That amount is charged on the individual mortgage. As I say, no inspection work has been done because in some cases there is only a basement. There could not possibly be any decision as to whether the plans and specifications have been followed. It looks to me like plain highway robbery. People are being fleeced out of their money and that should not be permitted.
I would rather see an inspection fee of $100 charged, provided qualified inspectors were employed and were carrying out their duties properly. I do not think that would be too much to pay to see that the houses are built according to the plans and specifications. I am not criticizing the size of the fee; I am criticizing the niggardly way in which it is *earned.
As has been pointed out, it was not earned at all, it was just a clear case of stealing. It would be worth while to have a proper inspector inspect these buildings. If that were done the government would save money and so would the people. The other day the hon. member for Halton said that he did not see why the minister should be so cautious as to bring forward amendments which the whole house except the hon. member thought were worth while in order to safeguard people who are taking advantage of this National Housing Act. The hon. member referred to the little affair in Calgary which caused all the commotion, but that is not so. The conditions that exist in Calgary exist all over Canada. All the hon. member for Halton has to do is to pick up the daily newspaper and he will see that they exist right here in Ottawa.
Why? As I have said so many times, it is that the government has not competent inspectors. The whole blame right here in Ottawa can be laid to that fact. I am not critical of the $20 inspection fee. As I say, I would gladly make it $100 provided a proper inspection was made of these places. It is not too late for the minister to take that into consideration and see that these inspectors really earn their money. It would save the people of this country millions of dollars and would save the government a lot of headaches.
Has the minister an answer to my first question with regard to the twenty-five per cent holdback? He has seen the pamphlets and I am sure he agrees that I read them properly, and I should like some explanation.

Under the amendments to the act I understand the government intends to allow a certain percentage of the loan for the labour put into the building of the home. of a co-operative. That places the group and the individual in a position where they must secure other credit.

At this moment it is difficult to know whether the questions 1 wish to ask and the remarks I wish to make are going to be relevant in all cases, but I hope that you, Mr. Chairman, will be as lenient with me as you have been with other speakers.
The city of London is no different from most of the other communities in Canada; we are suffering from growing pains. One of the difficulties that I have encountered is between the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the insurance company that is making the loan, the contractor and the owner or the owner-to-be. It would seem that the crux of all the difficulty is the inadequate inspection from time to time. As the purchaser of a home, because of the fact that it is a Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation project, with the government behind it, I expect that it is going to be all right. Purchasers are disappointed when they find that such is not the case.
There are some difficulties. I must admit that in London the type of housing that is being built is I think superior to that which is being built probably anywhere else in Canada, according to what I have heard. But these small difficulties occur. Possibly if better inspections were made, those difficulties would be ironed out. But when a number of complaints were given to me about these particular homes, and when I took the matter up with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and with the insurance company,

each of them passed the buck. They said: This was done two or three years ago, and the timber shrinks, and that is the reason that these difficulties occur.
I just want to point out what happens when a man applies for a loan for a home under the National Housing Act. I am going to read three paragraphs that are on the application and questionnaire. The first is as follows:
Borrowers and purchasers must make their own arrangements with the builder or vendor ot the house and must not assume that their interests have been or are being looked after by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or the lending institution making the loan.
I do not suppose that one in a dozen actually knows that paragraph is in there. Then there is another paragraph which reads as follows:
The lending company collects from the borrower $20 for the appraisal of the property and a minimum of four (4) inspections of the house during construction. These inspections are to see that C.M.H.C. standards are complied with, and to determine when progress advances may be made on the mortgage. They do not assure a full architectural or engineering inspection to see that all details of the plans and specifications are complied with.
What is the use of hiring an inspector if he does not look after these things? The last paragraph reads:
There have been instances in the past where borrowers and purchasers have made no contract with the builder and made no inspections of the house because they relied on the fact that they were getting "an N.H.A. house." This is a warning to borrowers and purchasers that they must make their own contract with vendors or builders and look after their own interests and inspections in the building or acquisition of a home.
That lets the lending institution, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and everyone else out from under. The only man who is going to be responsible is the man who buys the house. When he moves in and finds these defects he is troubled about them. I maintain that when a man accepts a house an itemized list should be made of all the different things in the house, and then an inspection should be made and each of these items checked off so that when the man takes the house he has agreed that it is as it should be. The owner and purchaser should sign that acceptance document. If the person who is acquiring the property did that he would know where he was, and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the lending institution would be protected.
I want to say a word or two about integrated housing and prefabricated housing in London. Generally I think they are doing a good job. In fact I know of instances where from $700 to $1,000 is being saved to owners of these particular houses in London; but still these defects sometimes show up and they
National Housing Act
cause bad feeling, shall I say, between the builder, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and the purchaser. One of the advantages they are finding there is a saving in taxes and insurance. Perhaps that is not possible under some other plans. I just want to mention what Central Mortgage and Housing had to say when I complained of some of these defects. One of the things I complained about was the wiring, and this is what they say:
The electric wiring could no doubt have been improved-
I complained about the defect of switches on the stairway. They would not work both ways. If you were upstairs and wanted to turn on the light downstairs it would not work. This is the reply I got.
The electric wiring could no doubt have been improved but it would fall into the category of a "frill" as mentioned above.
I think that is a necessity in every properly-wired house. This is their second comment:
It is quite possible that there may be a few visible leaks in the cold air ducts, after being installed this length of time. In the process of wood drying out there might be a tendency of it pulling away from the metal duct. However, the average new home owner expects minor defects like that and usually it is no trick for a minor repair.
To say the least, I think that is a silly statement. I do not agree with it.
Then there was the question of ice forming on the steps. I complained of that. Their comment was:
In so far as entrance steps are concerned, we considered they were adequate, and again one must consider the price at which these houses were sold.
It does not cost any more to put a cement step in right than it does to put it in wrong. When I took it up with the lending institution this is what they said:
In spite of what is said on this form, we do our best to give reasonable consideration to any difficulties that borrowers may have.
I do not want to go into all the details, but it was just as I mentioned in the beginning, namely, passing the buck. The man has his house and nobody is going to do anything about it. There are defects there but he is stuck with it and nothing can be done. As far as humanly possible we should encourage the people to own their own homes. That is very desirable in this country. We want a country of property owners. They are the backbone of the country. Let us do all we can to foster that. The hon. member for Nipissing mentioned that in his speech a few days ago.
When speaking on the resolution stage of this bill the hon. member for Spadina made a reference to subsidized housing, and hoped that it would be brought into effect. I hold in my hand a clipping from the Montreal

National Housing Act
Gazette of November 11, 1949. They quoted from the big green book of the Department of National Revenue, released on that day. The heading of the report is as follows: "Report shows only 540 farmers in Quebec assessed for income." The remark I want to make is that all the other farmers in the province of Quebec will be paying for subsidized housing in any city to which it is applied. I do not think that is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR JOINT OPERATION OF HOUSING PROJECTS AND LOANS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think perhaps I should make a statement about inspection. I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member, although I think they are considerably wide of this section; but in the circumstances we are all glad to have them. I think he would expect me to say with respect to his remark about passing the buck that the normal assumption of responsibility and the expectation that people will assume their normal responsibility is not, in my opinion, passing the buck. It seems to me, though, that there has been a great tendency for people to expect some departure from the normal relationship between the purchaser of a house and the builder of that house or the mortgagee, whichever the case may be; and if that relationship does not obtain in all respects the first recourse is to the government. Then, if the government does not come in and bail out the home owner, the immediate charge is one of passing the buck.
This is quite a long statement on the inspection procedure, but in view of the fact that the point has been raised I think I should read it.
For the most part loans under the National Housing Act are made jointly by approved lending institutions and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The arrangement between the lending institution and the corporation is set down in an agreement between them which deals with the administration of the loan, both during the process of construction and thereafter during the period of repayment. The lending institution takes charge of the administration of the loan and the agreement provides that during the period of construction the lending institution shall inspect the house as often as will reasonably ensure that the owner or builder is properly and faithfully carrying out a work of construction in accordance with the plans and specifications approved by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The agreement specifies that such inspections shall, in any event, be not less frequent than:
(a)	once at or before the laying of the footings,
(b)	once at or before the time when the roof is completed,
[Mr. White (Middlesex Eastl.1
(c)	once prior to the process of lathing or its equivalent, and
(d)	once on completion of the house.
In addition to the above-mentioned inspections the agreement provides that the corporation may make additional inspections, and the corporation in fact does, from time to time, follow through on inspections of houses which are being financed jointly under the National Housing Act for the purpose of seeing that the terms of the operating agreement are being fulfilled.
I should like to make it clear that in the matter of inspections no attempt is being made to shift responsibility from the corporation to the lending institution or vice versa. The government feels that the inspections which are made are not intended to provide full architectural inspections and supervision. The borrower pays $20 for the appraisal of his lot and the inspections which are made. A full architectural inspection, and supervision of the house would normally cost not less than $150.
We have endeavoured to make our position clear to borrowers under the National Housing Act, and have printed on the questionnaire, which is the first document that a prospective home owner sees, and the sales form, which is the first document that a prospective purchaser sees, a warning which deals with the corporation's position regarding inspections. For the information of hon. members I should like to read the warning as it appears on the documents I have mentioned:

Warning to Borrowers or Purchasers
Borrowers and purchasers must make their own arrangements with the builder or vendor of the house and must not assume that their interests have been or are being looked after by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or the lending institution making the loan.
That is the same section as was read by the hon. member for Middlesex East.
In the case of a purchaser of a completed house, the purchaser must satisfy himself that the house is. up to the standard that he thinks he is getting.
In the case of a purchaser of a house under construction, the purchaser must himself see that the portion built is up to the standard he thinks he is getting, and that the remainder of the house is completed as arranged between him and the builder..
Borrowers likewise must make their own arrangement with a contractor and see that the house is built according to the plans and specifications which have been agreed upon between the borrower and the contractor.
The lending company collects from the borrower $20 for the appraisal of the property and a minimum of four inspections of the house during construction. These inspections are to see that C.M.H.C. standards are complied with, and to determine when progress advances may be made on the

mortgage. They do not assure a full architectural or engineering inspection to see that all details of the plans and specifications are complied with.
There have been instances in the past where borrowers and purchasers have made no contract with the builder and made no inspections of the house because they relied on the fact that they were getting an N.H.A. house. This is a warning to borrowers and purchasers that they must make their own contract with vendors or builders and look after their own interests and inspections in the building or acquisition of a home.
The National Housing Act is designed to provide credit to assist prospective home owners in acquiring their homes, credit which cannot be obtained through normal commercial channels. The interest rate is lower than the prevailing rate and the terms of repayment of the loan are much more favourable than those normally given. To add the responsibility of making complete architectural inspections upon the lenders would impose a burden almost impossible to discharge, and most certainly would increase the over-all cost to the borrower resulting from the discharge of such responsibility.
As hon. members know, since 1935, joint loans have accounted for approximately 100,000 units. This has meant 400,000 inspections at least so far. In the year 1949 there are being built under the National Housing Act at least 30,000 units, calling for 120,000 inspections.
It seems to me that we can go no further on the inspections than we do at the present time and at the same time take all steps Possible to inform borrowers of their responsibilities and ours in connection with this problem.

I should like to compliment the minister and his officials upon this section in the bill, namely the one referring to home owners. This very day I received a letter from the minister as a result of my drawing his attention to a certain case in Capreol concerning a man earning $3,800 a year, who had applied to all the lending institutions in the country and could not get a loan to build his own home. This man is certainly in a position to be a home owner in Canada.
I believe the section before us will take care of a matter of that kind. I do not like situations such as that of the man in Capreol who had to go 150 miles to get help with his house. Sudbury is one of the most thriving cities in Ontario. It is sixth largest in the province; yet there is no office of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation there. Despite this, we find them in many smaller centres of Ontario where I should think they would not be as necessary as they are in Sudbury.
National Housing Act
In Sudbury we have I believe the largest payroll for individual men of any city in Canada. Many of our men are earning from $300 to $400 a month. These people want to-become home owners in Sudbury, and they have no way of finding out how they can get those homes. They are refused the help of lending institutions-why, I cannot say. This-is more serious than one might think. I am one who was refused the help of a lending institution. I am also one who is paying monthly to the national housing administration in Canada for my own home. But I was refused my home until such time as I refused to take "No" for an answer from these big financiers. I came to Ottawa and discussed my problem with the officials here. The man who was in charge of the national housing administration in 1938 told me that if those lending institutions did not accept my application they would not receive any more applications from anybody else. He believed I was certainly one who could comply with the regulations surrounding the buying of a home in my town of Sudbury.
Next morning upon my return to Sudbury the representative of the lending institution was waiting for me, with a taxi, at the station, to take me home, and to tell me that I was going to be given a loan. He did not have to do that, because I had already been told that the day before in Ottawa.
This goes to show that these lending institutions are not serving the purpose and the spirit of national housing in this country. They are taking the cream of the loans in all' sections. Furthermore, I would add that they zone certain sections of the city because they have streets in these localities in which they own real estate; and if you do not build a home in that section you cannot get a loan through these people.
I do not think Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should or will stand for any of this. Let me say to the minister now that the sooner his department establishes an office in Sudbury, the better. In three or four months they will have no regrets for having done so, because there are many people there who are able to come within the regulations; and build their own homes.

Mr. Chairman, I shall try to confine my brief remarks to this section of the bill. May I associate myself with others in thanking the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply for having brought this bill before-the House of Commons. It is a step in the right direction, and I believe it will accelerate the building of homes throughout Canada.
One angle of the bill, however, I think will' not work out as satisfactorily as might be hoped. I refer to its application to the smaller

National Housing Act
towns and villages throughout Canada. Under the old act we could negotiate an additional loan up to $1,250 as a second mortgage. That, of course, is not possible under the new. All hon. members realize that the lending value depends upon different factors in different sections of the country. The rental value of a property may depend upon the amount of money a wage-earner makes, and also upon other factors. The lending value in the small towns and villages is not as great as the lending value in the cities. As we all know, the basic loan is 80 per cent of the lending value and consequently people in the towns and villages are not going to be able to secure as much money by way of loans.
Apparently the lending institutions are not willing to go out from the cities in order to negotiate loans in the small urban centres. The reason is quite apparent. The cost of inspecting and supervision of a property 50 or 60 miles away from the office of the lending institution is considerable. But this is something that could be overcome. I believe the minister has a humanitarian feeling for the people across Canada. The housing situation in the cities is quite acute but I think at times that is over-emphasized. There is a housing shortage in the towns and villages where a large proportion of our population reside.
As the hon. member for Eglinton told us the other night, this is a social problem of great magnitude. As he said, this should be a pilgrimage to a happy land. I am quite sure the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply will take this matter into consideration. I think it was the hon. member for Lambton West who stated the other evening that the interest rate on loans should be reduced to three and a half per cent. I am sure the minister will take that into consideration also. So if by sound legislation we can remove every obstruction and impediment that will interfere with the construction of homes for *our people, we will win the acclaim of our citizens from sea to sea and justify by this action alone the sittings of the house for this fall session.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to support the remarks of the two previous speakers with respect to the service given by the lending institutions to the small towns and villages.

These remarks have nothing to do with this particular subsection. If we are going to get into a general discussion we should revert to the proper section. We are now on section 2, subsection 1.
Subsection 1 agreed to.

On subsection 2.

There are two phases to this subsection, one having to do with the percentage and the other having to do with the lending value.
So far as percentage is concerned I can understand that a flat rate of 80 per cent has the virtue of simplicity, but I do not think that is what dictated this amendment.
1	fancy the reason the government is proposing to depart from the present standards of 95 per cent for the first $2,000 of lending value, 85 per cent for the next $2,000, and 70 per cent for everything above that is that houses in the low-price range are not being built today. I should like to ask the minister if calculations have been made to indicate how the 80 per cent will compare with the present basis of granting loans. My impression is that it will work out just about the same, but perhaps the minister has some figures on that point.
I turn now to the question of lending value which in many respects is a vital matter. There is not much use our preparing great plans to help house construction if we are going to write down the lending value. Lending value is defined in subsection 23 of section
2	of the act as follows:
"Lending value" means the estimated cost of construction or cost of conversion, or the appraised value, whichever is less, of a house or housing project.
In other words, in the case of a new house, "lending value" as defined by the act is the estimated cost of construction or the appraised value, whichever is less. I have said before, and I repeat, that the interpretation which has been placed upon lending value in the administration of this act has subtracted greatly from the intended effectiveness of the act. We know perfectly well that the definition put upon lending value by those responsible for the administration of this act has not borne a direct relationship to the cost of construction today.
This is not the first time this matter has been discussed. The minister's predecessor was pressed on this matter more than once, and his answer was that there would not be any departure from the practice of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, that they were not going to measure lending value in terms of the cost of construction. While building costs have been steadily mounting during the lifetime of this act, lending value as interpreted by those responsible for administering the act has not risen proportionately.

I think that those responsible for administering the act have been putting too much emphasis upon the fear of inflation in housing values. They have been more bent upon avoiding loss in connection with lending operations than they have been on making this section fruitful in the construction of new homes. The administration can reduce the effectiveness of the act if they are not going to measure the lending value in terms of modern costs of construction. I say that there should be a more sympathetic interpretation of lending value in the future than there has been in the past; otherwise we are going to see much of the effectiveness of this act taken from it by those responsible for the administration.
I think the minister is prepared to concede that costs of production have been rising, although they have reached some measure of stabilization in recent months, and those responsible for administering the act should be ready to abandon this fear of inflation which has apparently beset them in the past. I urge upon the minister a change of heart and a change of emphasis in connection with this matter.
There are many people who have good reason to complain that they have received less by way of mortgage loan under this act than parliament intended they should receive. I think the reason for that has been unsympathetic administration. I ask the minister to make up his mind and perhaps give the committee assurance that from now on lending value is going to have a direct relationship to the cost of construction and not to some fictitious figure which has the effect of writing down the lending value.

With much of what the hon. member has said I agree. He has said that a certain attitude with respect to lending value has been taken by those administering the act. He thought that the administration in some respects was throttling the intent of the act. In fairness to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, I think I should say that the government has at all times been informed by the corporation of these matters of administration, and they have carried the judgment of the government. I feel the time has come for some revision of the attitude towards lending values, and in that I am in entire agreement with what the hon. member has said.

Does Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation determine the lending value of the property, or is it the company that lends the money?
National Housing Act
They are joint loans, and the decision is a joint decision, but the lending institution predominates in the loan, and it would have the greater voice in the decision.

Would it not have practically the controlling voice? Is it not true that the lending company decides whether it will lend anything, and how much it will lend, regardless of what the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has to say?
In agreements and arrangements between the lending institution and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation there is no point of difference with respect to that problem.

Will the minister be kind enough to deal with the first point I raised? I asked a question about how the 80 per cent is going to compare in the future with the way the blended percentages have worked out up to the present time.

The 80 per cent will be approximately equivalent to the average loan under the present arrangement, and the extra one-sixth under the new arrangement will have the effect of reducing the amount of the down payment required by approximately one-half.

Subsection agreed to.
On subsection 3.

I do not think anyone will object to increasing the period in question to thirty years provided at least two conditions are present. One is sound methods of construction and the other point is one on which I now ask assurance that it will not be overlooked. The section as it stands now contemplates that there shall be protection of the area by community planning and appropriate zoning restrictions. No reference is made to that healthy safeguard in the proposed amended form of the subsection. It may be unnecessary, but I would ask the minister for his explicit assurance that that necessary form of protection is not going to be overlooked, and that due emphasis will be placed upon protection by means of community planning and proper zoning restrictions.

As the hon. member has said, subsection 3 of section 2 may give the appearance that we are abandoning the principle of the desirability of community planning and zoning. This is far from the case because in the ordinary operations of loans under the National Housing Act the areas in which loans are made are limited to those which are

National Housing Act
stable and have every possibility of remaining good residential neighbourhoods during the term of the loan.
The limitation now contained in the act, that loans for a term exceeding twenty-five .years but not in excess of thirty years shall be limited to areas protected by community planning and appropriate zoning restrictions, presents administrative difficulties. With higher costs of construction and the larger loans provided in the amendments, it is likely that longer terms of amortization will require that the debt service on the larger loans be kept within a reasonable percentage of the owner's income. Debt service includes principal, interest and taxes. Generally the corporation is unwilling to approve an individual as a satisfactory home owner where the debt service exceeds 23 per cent of the 'owner's income.
There are a number of communities which *are quite satisfactory from the residential point of view in which there is no approved community plan. The practicalities of the situation are that in some cases in these communities a thirty-year amortization is required. Provided that there are adequate :zoning restrictions and the location is satisfactory, there is no reason why loans on a thirty-year basis should not be made. I question the advisability at this time of using the limitation to a shorter term of amortization as a method to force municipalities to approve a community plan. There are more effective ways of achieving this end without imposing a hardship upon individuals whose circumstances make a thirty-year loan desirable.
I may say that in considering applications for loans under the National Housing Act an area rating is considered. The basis of this rating takes into account all features relating to the community. If the rating is high there is no reluctance in proceeding with a thirty-year amortization. If, however, the rating is low, amortization will be restricted to fifteen or twenty years. In principle we believe that the community planning restriction has much merit. From a practical point of view, however, we believe that administrative procedures can better achieve the purposes of the present limitation.

I should like to point out that what has just been said raises one of the serious objections to the National Housing Act. It limits loans to people with relatively high incomes and stability of occupation or work. The kind of housing that is most needed is that for people who have not high incomes, and who have not any great assurance of continued work. Where loans are made it is usually in a high-class district in

the community. In our cities there are numerous working class districts, as they are termed, and it is impossible for people living there to get a loan under the National Housing Act, no matter how good the character of the individual. Steadiness of employment, even if the wage is not high, should be a factor in obtaining a loan under the act, but I do not think that applies at all unless there is an assurance of a certain level of income. As a matter of fact, the National Housing Act as it has been operated up till now helps those to build homes who most likely could do so without the National Housing Act at all.

Just before six o'clock I think I should say that one of the greatest limiting factors in the areas the hon. member for Vancouver East has just mentioned is the unavailability of land. I would say to him, however, on a more encouraging note, that the dominion-provincial arrangements contemplate scope for operation in those fields.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.
