The house resumed from Tuesday, November 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Benidickson for the second reading of Bill No. 119, to incorporate Prairie Transmission Lines Limited, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Maclnnis.

Mr. Speaker, when one of these bills was last before us, I made a number of references to what the legal position was. In this House of Commons, we have gone on the assumption that a statement made by the Prime Minister that the export of gas in Alberta was purely a matter for the provincial government was true; but with great respect and deference,
I have ventured to disagree. For a moment I should like to speak about the statements that have been loosely made, not only loosely made but falsely made if they included myself, to the effect that I was taking part in a filibuster. My immediate answer to that is that-I see some amusement registered by the member for Leeds (Mr. Fulford). I think he should stay with his cheese production, and not stick his nose into things he knows nothing about. The fact is that I made a speech on the other bill, and tonight I am making a speech on this one. That will be the end of my efforts, irrespective of amendments or anything of that kind.
Prairie Transmission Lines
In my own favour, I think I may safely say that that can scarcely be called a filibuster; particularly when the gas we are talking about originates in the province in which I have lived for over forty years, and I am really interested in what happens to that gas.
The hon. Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) made a speech on one of these bills. He is not only the hon. Minister of Fisheries, he is one of my oldest, closest and best-regarded friends. He made some reference to statements which I had made, and suggested that I did not know what I was talking about. He began by saying that I referred to only one pipe line, and I quote his words as they appear at page 2019 of Hansard:
Then he went on to say that this pipe line should be built on Canadian soil. I think he should he asked to give us his authority for making such a definite statement to the house.
I made that statement, and now I give my authority. I begin by giving you, Mr. Speaker, a statement made by Mr. Dixon in the evidence given before the Senate on one of these bills. I am afraid I must confuse these bills to some extent, but the principle is exactly the same. This is the man behind the other bill, and at page F-3 he said this in answer to a question by Hon. Mr. MacKinnon:
No, that would be utterly impossible. You could not finance the line. This is the way it will have to be regulated. We shall make contracts to sell gas in Vancouver, Seattle and Portland, and we shall have to have sufficient gas for the entire market or the line will not be financed. If the gas should play out, which is inconceivable, Vancouver would naturally get the last gas.
I read that slowly and quietly to you, because those are the words of the man almost entirely responsible for that bill. The member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness), when this particular bill was before the house, read a statement-required by statute-from the newspapers in Calgary, which said definitely the route was through Kingsgate into the United States, on to those American cities and then to Vancouver at the tail end of the line. Now, Mr. Speaker and hon. members, I am not going to abuse any company. I pause to make this statement with respect to the bill we passed last session. I think we acted like schoolboys. We did not make a proper examination of that bill, and my responsibility is the same as that of the other members in this house. May I say that if the board of transport commissioners, before whom that company is now, imposes a condition that the line be built on Canadian soil I shall welcome it. I do not want to leave any doubt in anyone's mind as to why I am adopting the position I am.
Then, in further support of my answer to the statement made by the hon. Minister

Prairie Transmission Lines of Fisheries, that they wanted to allow the prospective company's lines through to Vancouver-it was three lines, I think-
No, I mentioned two.

-two gas lines, I read the statement of Mr. Connolly, who is a king's counsel, and who appeared before a Senate committee. At page C-5 he said this:
It is necessary to include the United States market because the limited market available in Canada would not, in itself, support the cost of a pipe line from any of the known Canadian natural gas fields to Vancouver.
I have quoted to you statements made by spokesmen of both these corporations, who were speaking with full authority. They demonstrate that there will be no gas line except one which will take care of this whole market. There can be no doubt of that. In that testimony, there is a good deal of evidence as to the quantities which will be required over a twenty-five-year period. It amounts to so many trillions of cubic feet that it staggers me. I notice something which I thought amusing in the evidence given before the committee, and that is that in London a trillion is a million million, while in New York it is a hundred thousand million. In other words, the word "trillion" has two definitions in the mathematics of those two countries. When the committee was finished, it did not appear to be definite whether they were using the London measurement or the New York measurement. So I leave that because the Minister of Lands and Mines in Alberta, Mr. Tanner, made a statement the other day which we have all read. He said that there would be no export of gas from Alberta unless the supply in Alberta were assured for fifty years. That is quite a statement to make, but what does it mean? Frankly, in my judgment, it does not mean much. Who is to prognosticate the progress in that province and who, therefore, can do any more than guess how many trillions of feet we need to have now, using either measurement, to take care of that province for the next fifty years?
The minister asked me where I got my authority for that statement. I have quoted to him the top officers of one of these companies. Then may I say to him that I have further authority, and I do not mean secondhand information. I have authority from the firm of Ford, Bacon and Davis of New York city, the largest engineering firm in the world, who told me it was utterly silly to think of more than one pipe line to this one market from the oil fields of Alberta. I will not mention the gentleman's name but I saw him some little time ago in the hotel in which I

think the minister and I are both living. If he wants further authority, I will give him privately the name of a man who stands all by himself in North America as a gas engineer. He assured me of the same thing. If that is not enough, I want to give him the names of two prominent senators who certainly are not of my political persuasion. One is Senator Farris.
Order.

The other is Senator Turgeon. Am I out of order, Mr. Speaker? If I am, I will stop; but I did not think that I was. May I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that I was merely answering a question put to me by his colleague, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew). I hope there will not be another cabinet split over that. Let us try to get along without that necessity.
The hon. member went on and gave us these routes. Then he said that they should follow the routes taken by the Canadian National Railways and the Great Northern Railway. Into this I have also made some inquiry, but I want to ask my good friend the Minister of Fisheries a question. In the mountain section all railways run through tunnels. They run through tunnels only because there is no overland route. In their evidence before the Senate, these people say that they expect to carry this gas at a pressure of 750 pounds as opposed to the pressure at sea level which we all know is fifteen pounds. I should like to ask the minister how he would like to travel through a tunnel on a train knowing that he has a 24-inch gas line underneath him carrying gas at a pressure of 750 pounds. Connaught tunnel is five miles long. This is on the C.P.R. One can just imagine what would happen to the minister and the rest of the train if there was some accident with respect to the gas carried at a pressure of 750 pounds through these tunnels which are on all these railways. It is not a matter of the C.P.R. or anything like that.
There is nearly that much pressure under the minister now.

The hon. member suggests there is that much pressure under him now. I think there is more than that on him, not under. Then the minister said:
As Canadians we should be supplied first with the gas we need and then, just the same as with anything else, we should export our surplus. II we have a surplus of gas and oil then I say we have every right to export it unless we want to build a fence around ourselves and become isolated from everybody else.

In that statement let me compliment the minister. He has put the truth simply and forcefully and much better than I might ever do it myself. Then he went on and, speaking of me, he said:
I should like to tell the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) that, when the first oil field was drilled in the province of Alberta, when people thought it was a wild gamble and there was no oil in the Turner valley, some of my money was invested in that project taking a long chance.
I think the minister will admit that he did it, as I will admit that I did it; and how many thousand other suckers, including myself, were pinched in on that particular occasion? I am sure he will remember this incident, because he was in Calgary then. The name of the company I have forgotten, but it was operated by a fellow by the name of Buck. I think the Minister of Fisheries was probably in that show too.
No, I was not.
The minister *was smarter than I was.
Black Diamond.

I remember that show well. There was some gas in this hole. A number of us enthusiasts went down there. Buck had salted the well with machine oil. There is no doubt about that. So enthusiastic were we that we-I even in my Sunday clothes-stood under it, stunk like a skunk and had this stuff poured all over us. We thought Mr. Buck had a big well. I am glad the Minister of Fisheries was not in there. But I gather that the Minister of Trade and Commerce might have had a share or two.
I think I have finished dealing with the speech of the minister. He mentioned, as other people have, the word "monopoly". In the first speech I made in connection with this matter I too said there could be, economically, only one 24-inch or 26-inch pipe line. In his evidence, Mr. Dixon admits that it must be at least a 26-inch pipe line. In the carriage of gas, if you have a 12-inch line it will carry so much; and if you have a 24-inch line it carries five times as much. In other words, you just cannot say 4, 8, 12, 16, 24 inches and so on. You must remember that the gas takes in the whole circumference of the pipe, and a 24-inch line will carry five times as much gas as a 12-inch line will carry.
What is our position out there with respect to gas? I have read the telegram. I am anxious that my Social Credit friends should know this. I have read the telegram from Mr. Manning. I have read the statement made the other day by Mr. Tanner, the minister of lands and mines. Both of those gentlemen are fine and able men. What have they said?
Prairie Transmission Lines They have said that they have a policy of Albertans first, Canadians second and other people third. These are their priorities. In my judgment nobody in the world, at least none of us who come from there, would dare dispute that simple statement. But Mr. Manning did say that he was not opposed to the incorporation of other companies, thereby having a better chance for bids to do this particular job. Neither will I dispute that.
We have before us two applications. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is a great authority on these matters. The other night I heard him say-and I am sure he meant it-that he controlled the export of gas beyond Canada. I agreed with him; I still agree. But to be realistic we must know that when this tremendous amount of money has been spent we have a situation confronting us that means something. One gas line company frankly admits that in the event of a breakdown or a shortage Vancouver will be at the end of the line and will suffer first because of the contracts they will have made with the northwestern United States and clearly and most important with the cities of Seattle and Portland. Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to pause here because I am leaving the filibuster business out. I want to pause and ask hon. members this question: Do they want that, if the main scheme can be accomplished in some other way?
I have read the evidence very carefully. We know that we have been told that five lines were looked at by one company. We have been told by Mr. Dixon that to build a line on Canadian soil, that is just north of the border, would cost $20 million more than if it crosses at Kingsgate, runs through the United States and turns up with the last bit of gas to Vancouver. I wonder, sir, whether hon. members will not pause and consider. Is it not more worth while that Mr. Dixon, a man from New York, described as an engineer and geologist, and I am sure he is, should build a line through Canada? Is it not much more important to us that Canadians should have the advantage of that line rather than save Mr. Dixon $20 million? The sum of $20 million is not a great deal in a $125 million proposition. Roughly that is to be the cost of this project. So far as I am concerned- I do not go to Vancouver often because it rains out there all the time-I do not care how much it costs Mr. Dixon, but I do care about Vancouver being on the front end of this pipe line and not on the tail end of it. That, Mr. Speaker, is the simple problem that hon. members have to decide when this comes to a vote, and I have already promised that I shall not further hinder that vote after I have concluded my remarks this evening.

Prairie Transmission Lines
What is the position? I am trying to bring this thing down to what we are going to vote on, because we shall vote on it some day. I am going to tell the house this because I am anxious to justify myself completely in regard to the attitude I have taken on these bills. I begin by saying, suppose someone came here and asked for a charter to build a railway and did not tell us where the railway was to go. He would be laughed out of the House of Commons. 1 do not think I shall hear a voice dissenting from that statement. If hon. gentlemen have not seen the last issue of Fortune magazine I would ask them to take a look at some of the maps in it showing the underlying gas lines in the United States. If they do so they will see that they are infinitely more plentiful in certain areas than are railroads. The underground pipe lines of the United States, both gas and oil, have a far greater mileage than all the railways in the United States. The last issue of Fortune may be procured in the library. I had it for only a minute or two. It shows the tremendous development. In other words, the development of gas as a fuel is far ahead of coal or of fuel oil. The curves on the graphs in this magazine show that the price of gas is infinitely more on a level line than either of the other two, which are going up. Those of you who burn oil and coal even in your houses will know the truth of what I speak. It would be very interesting for hon. members to look at Fortune magazine to see the expansion of the pipe line business, which has now become a major business in the United States. It will become so in this country.
I am not one of those who believe that in Alberta we have all the gas in Canada. I am certain we have not. I know that in the Peace river area, particularly of British Columbia, they have lots of gas. Incidentally, within the last ten days in that country, the Pacific Petroleum Company-I do not mind mentioning their name-have brought in two excellent gas wells across the British Columbia border. I think they are in the constituency of the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray). I may be wrong about that. I am anxious that we should not fail to give this matter proper consideration. Let us have some facts with respect to the whole problem, because we are only on the doorstep of the development of the oil and gas industry in Canada.
We come now to what I think is our real problem, and in my judgment our only problem. The other night I mentioned what a tremendously useful purpose this line would serve in northern Alberta and in northern British Columbia. At the moment these

areas are undeveloped. Let me put it this way. The development could be infinitely greater if they had some form of energy such as natural gas. I am not insisting on that route or that company or on any other company, but I am saying-and perhaps this is what we shall vote on-that we are going to vote on whether this is or is not a Canadian line. I for one will oppose anything which is not a Canadian line.
I pause to take up the answers to that question. The answers so far given are that we have the board of transport commissioners. We have the province of Alberta with certain authority, and they will not permit this or that because they have announced as a policy Albertans first, Canadians second and other people third in priority.
What are we doing here? We saw fit to pass-and everybody has agreed with that- a Pipe Lines Act. The principal provision of that act is that people going to do that must procure their charter by private act of this parliament. But for that, anybody could go to the Secretary of State and get letters patent with a big red seal, and green ribbons hanging down from it, permitting him to incorporate a company of any description-the only exception being that the company be not incorporated for illegal purposes. In other words, you could not incorporate a gambling club, as such. But for any other divisions of human activity you can get incorporation from the dominion government, simply by procuring letters patent.
We saw fit to change all that. We saw fit to say that in connection with a gas line they must come to the House of Commons. Why did we do that? We did it in order that this House of Commons-this thing being of such importance-should make an examination of the problem or proposition which was submitted.
Now then, if we today are to incorporate gas pipe lines without knowing where they are going, or over what route, we become nothing but a rubber stamp-just the same rubber stamp as used by the Secretary of State when we could incorporate for any purposes at all. Surely that is true. Surely there is no argument against the simple statement I have made.
Order-

I conclude bysaying this-I saw you getting nervous, sir, and I think I have come to my conclusion at about the same time. We passed one pipe line bill last spring, and I think we were foolish. I am content, because that is the company about which some people in this House of Commons have been circulating the

rumour that I am in that picture. If I were outside I would know what to call them- and I do not see anybody where I am looking at the moment.
But I do say this, that 1 am content now to say that the transport board in dealing with their application, which will come up within the next month or two, should put in that permission the proviso that that company must complete their line on Canadian soil. I am quite content and happy that that should be done.
And so I say to the sponsor of this bill- and they are both together, both this bill and the other one-that if they will take a little piece of paper, and put on it only one line, saying that this company shall build this line between Alberta and Vancouver, and that it shall go on Canadian soil, I will join in making it unanimous with all the members of this House of Commons; and that bill will not meet with any more trouble, and we shall not have any more stupid, silly and false charges of filibustering in connection with this matter. That is all I have to say.

Before six o'clock the hon. member for Bow River asked me a question concerning two pamphlets issued by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation having to do with the integrated housing plan. He will notice one of the pamphlets is dated July, 1947, and the other one June, 1948, and thus supersedes the former. The hon. member points out that there is a difference in these two pamphlets in respect of holdback. This is quite true because the terms and conditions of the integrated plan were changed which occasioned the issuing of a second booklet. The hon. member refers to a holdback of 25 per cent. We have no knowledge of such an amount because the usual holdback, where it is applicable, is in an amount of 15 per cent, not by regulation but in accordance with the appropriate mortgage practice.
It may be the hon. member is making the point that holdbacks in the case of houses built by the Bow River Construction Company should have been available for the benefit of home owners. I would point out that, even if the holdback were available, its purpose is not for the benefit of the home owner. The contract of the home owner is with the builder, and the lending institution looks to the house itself for its security. The discussion is quite academic, however, because the integrated housing plan was completely changed early in 1949 with title to the houses being transferred to the Central Mortgage

National Housing Act
and Housing Corporation at the joist stage. This change in the arrangement, although generally unacceptable to builders, has had the effect of protecting the position of the purchaser. The new plan requires that all down payments be trusteed. Under present arrangements, if trouble arises such as is described by the hon. member for Bow River, there is full protection to the purchaser of the house under the integrated housing plan. These changes, although improving the position of the home owner, have had the effect of greatly reducing the volume of houses produced under the integrated plan.
I hope that this answers the question of the hon. member. I do feel there is little purpose to be served in further debating what holdbacks were required two years ago, particularly when the holdbacks were not for the benefit of the individual purchasers in whom the hon. member is so interested. The hon. member also asked me whether there were regulations in respect of holdbacks in connection with the integrated plan. The National Housing Act requires regulations approved by the governor in council. I confirm that there are no regulations in this respect. The use of the word "regulations" in the pamphlet dated June, 1947, is a general one, and refers to mortgage procedure rather than to the formal regulations as required under the terms of the National Housing Act. I quite readily admit, Mr. Chairman, that the word in that sense is used loosely in the pamphlet. I should like to return the pamphlet to the hon. member.

The minister on an earlier occasion has very properly indicated that there is no thought in his mind of compelling the provinces to do things, but that his intention is that the act shall be administered with a view to assisting in co-operative endeavour with the provinces to find a solution in this particular branch of the housing field.

Lest hon. members may have formed the impression that all the provinces are just waiting to participate on these terms, I think it only right that we should have regard at this time to what the provinces themselves have said, particularly in view of the desirability and indeed the necessity of getting our feet on the ground on this problem, instead of running away with our heads in the clouds, as has been done with regard to this bill on some previous occasions by some hon. members.
I refer to the correspondence exchanged during the past year between the minister and the governments of the provinces with reference to this subject. I am going to refer only to the correspondence with two of the provinces, Alberta and Saskatchewan, because the governments of those provinces have written letters which I think should be before the committee. I do this in order to test some of the optimism that has been expressed by hon. members in connection with this bill.
According to the correspondence with Alberta I gather that when the minister made his statement in the house on September 21 the premier of Alberta made a public statement-the terms of that statement do not appear in this correspondence-which was apparently in rather critical terms. Thereupon the minister wrote to the premier of Alberta on September 24 expressing regret at his statement and saying that it must have been the result of some misunderstanding. He made reference to the correspondence

National Housing Act
which had been exchanged, and then on September 30 the premier of Alberta replied by letter from which I should like to quote as follows:
I, of course, do not know the contents of the press report reaching Ottawa but the statement I made to the press here was to the effect that I deplored the federal government's action in committing the provinces to participation, probably at heavy financial cost to the provinces, in any scheme not submitted beforehand for the approval of the provinces. I made no comment on the housing plan as such.
I have no hesitation in reiterating my objections to any plans requiring participation by the provinces and which is announced officially before the provinces have an opportunity to discuss and consider provisions of the plan at a round table conference. This is not the first time this has occurred. My own feeling in respect to the proper procedure is that in any plan formulated involving participation of the provinces, particularly financial participation, the federal government should call a conference of representatives of the provinces, submit the plan, invite discussion and by this means arrive at conclusions mutually satisfactory. It then would be time enough to announce the plan publicly.
In particular reference to the housing plan, even though the provinces are committed to 25 per cent of the costs, the provinces were given no opportunity to express favour or otherwise, or even submit alternative suggestions for joint dominion-provincial efforts to solve housing problems. It was our understanding your recent trip across Canada was of an exploratory nature to personally obtain information on the housing question and that this was preliminary to the calling of a meeting of dominion and provincial representatives to work out specific measures for coping with the problem.

Dear Mr. Manning:
Statements attributed to you by the Canadian Press following my announcement in the House of Commons on the 21st September would lead me to believe that there must be some misunderstanding. If this is in fact the case, I would like to submit the following record of correspondence and conversations between the Alberta government and the federal government in the hope that it may serve to clarify the situation.
March 2, 1949: The Prime Minister wrote you, enclosing my letter to him, the theme of both being that the federal government would welcome for consideration any suggestions or proposals your province might have with respect to its housing problem.
March 7, 1949:	You acknowledged the Prime
Minister's letter, stating that his communication was being brought to the attention of members of the government of Alberta.
April 8, 1949: I wrote you, stating that I would be absent from Ottawa during the period April 8 to April 25, and stated that if Alberta cared to submit suggestions in writing, they would be given early and full consideration.
July 30, 1949:	I wrote you, setting forth my
intention to visit Edmonton on August 23, and stating that I would welcome an opportunity of discussing the housing problem with you or your appropriate ministers.
August 5,	1949:	The Honourable Mr. N. E.
Tanner, acting premier, replied to my letter, stating it was unlikely that you would be available on the 23rd August, but that he had arranged for me to discuss the problem with the Honourable Mr. A. J. Hooke.
August 23, 1949:	In company with Mr. D. B.
Mansur, president, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and Mr. R. L. Elliott, private secretary, I had a full and pleasant discussion with the Honourable Mr. Hooke, who, as I understand it, stated that he was not able to express any definite views on behalf of his government but that he would bring the subject to the attention of his colleagues and inform them regarding our talk. At that time the proposals which were set before the House of Commons later on the 21st September were discussed quite fully.
September 1, 1949:	I wrote to the Honourable
Mr. Hooke, extending my appreciation for the opportunity to discuss the problem with him and expressing the hope that it would lead to a more comprehensive approach to the housing problem generally.
September 13, 1949:	I wrote to the Honourable
Mr. Hooke, outlining and crystallizing the discussions I had with him on the 23rd August and stating that I proposed to make a statement in the House of Commons along the same lines on or about September 20.
September 21, 1949:	I wrote the Honourable Mr. Hooke, enclosing a copy of the statement I made in the House of Commons on that day.
It is regretted that what appears to be a misunderstanding should have developed. I can assure you that it was most certainly not my intention or the intention of the federal government to proceed in this matter without first exchanging views with the government of Alberta. I was of the opinion that all possible steps had been taken to this end, and I was very pleased with the co-operative attitude reflected by the Honourable Mr. Hooke during our conversation.

It is my sincere hope that if there is a misunderstanding, this letter will serve to correct it. Moreover, if you would care to discuss the matter of housing more fully, I would welcome the opportunity.
Yours sincerely,
Robert H. Winters

This section of the act, Mr. Chairman, provides for the two governments jointly entering into a number of types of projects. First of all, it contemplates the assembly of land and services, and may not go beyond that. Another phase of it is that it enables the provincial and federal governments jointly to build on the land thus assembled. The houses built thereon may be sold or they may get into a rental position. From the outset, we have taken the view that the federal government does not wish to go further as a landlord, and that in any arrangement contemplating rental the management will be on a local basis. There will be some local housing authority.
We have said further that we wish to see as many houses as possible pass into ownership. We recognize that there are places where rental is required, and where people are able to pay economic rentals, economic rentals will be charged. The project will come under the management of the local housing authority. There is a further possibility that there may be rental housing required where the prospective tenants may not be able to pay economic rentals, in which case some underwriting of the losses might be required. We have said that we are prepared, jointly with the provincial governments on projects that are mutually acceptable, to underwrite those losses to the extent of 75 per cent federal money and 25 per cent provincial money.
In answer to the last question, about the relationship between this section and the slum clearance section which is already in the act, I would say that the two sections are entirely separate. That does not mean, however, that this section cannot be made operative with respect to a site that has been cleared and made available under the slum clearance section of the act.

National Housing Act Mr. Quelch: What will the rate of interest be? It seems to me that the government is placing in the housing scheme a very severe handicap when they maintain the rate of interest as high as they are under this act. I was interested in a press report appearing in the Christian Science Monitor of November 16, 1949, which states, under the heading "Low interest rates held rehousing aid"-
Mr. Bernard E. Loshbough, administrator of the Connecticut housing authority, stated:
"The housing plight of moderate income families is being met in a manner completely unique to this country. Low interest rates constitute the tool through which these houses are being made available to families, making too much for public housing ventures, yet not making enough to pay the current high rents or building costs."
Connecticut's plan of action was based upon a mortgage interest rate of only one and one-half per cent, made possible by state-backed credit. Thus lower interest rates constituted' the crux of the over-all Connecticut plan of providing for new housing.
Surely if the state of Connecticut is able to use its credit to provide money at the interest rate of one and a half per cent, the government of Canada, with the Bank of Canada at its disposal, should be able to finance the housing scheme at a very much lower cost than four and a half per cent interest.
I quite realize that the minister himself is not in a position to provide the money at that rate, but the government of Canada is. He should approach the government to try to provide money at a rate of interest which will really make it possible to have low rental housing in this country.

I just wanted to speak along the lines which had been followed by the two hon. members who preceded me and who were allowed by the Chairman to speak. I think I was perfectly in order but I was not allowed to say what I wanted to say at that time. Therefore, I shall say now what I intended to say then.
As I understand the principle of this bill, it is intended to provide more housing for Canadians. I support what was said this afternoon by two or three hon. members who said that they were of the opinion that those who live in small towns, in small villages and in rural communities do not receive from lending institutions the services they should receive under this act. I have had that very experience. I know that the small villages, the small towns and the rural communities in my constituency are not receiving the service they should receive from the lending institutions which operate under the act. I know of many good hard-working artisans, workmen, business people and others who have made applications for loans, who are well able to meet the payments on a decent type of house but whose applications have been rejected, mainly because they live in small towns, small villages or unincorporated areas.
From what I can gather, the objections of the lending institutions to lending money to people living in small towns, small villages and rural areas are, first, that they do not
National Housing Act
consider it to be a particularly good investment where the community is small and industry is not highly developed; second, they claim that quite often there is poor fire protection; third, they claim that the cost of inspection is greater.
With regard to the first objection, I contend that they are entirely wrong. Some of the most stable communities we have in this country are the small communities which stretch from one end of the country to the other. When it comes to poor fire protection I can speak from experience when I say that the small communities in my own constituency, particularly those with voluntary fire brigades, have a lower rate of fire loss than the larger centres. When they complain about high inspection costs I think they are failing completely to serve the Canadian people as they should. The lending institutions do very well under this act and I do not think they should be permitted to skim the cream and not serve the rural communities as they should.
In my opinion they are taking a coldblooded business view of this question, without any sense of their responsibilities to Canadians as a whole. In order to illustrate my point I should like to refer to what has happened in Nakusp, the village close by to where I live. This is a village of 750 population in the Arrow lakes. It is surrounded by wonderful scenery. It has a permanent forest industry based on a provincial forest which by means of selected logging will produce an annual yield of over thirty million board feet of lumber forever. In addition there is a well-established agricultural industry. This is a stable community which the people themselves have built up over the years.
In order to illustrate the financial strength of this small community and its position as a risk, I should like to mention some of the things that have been done by these people who want to have the opportunity under the act to borrow from lending institutions. This village of 750 people has a legion post with 25 members who have built and paid for completely a $20,000 community hall. They have built nine-hole golf course at a cost of between $5,000 and $7,000. They have built and paid for completely a $50,000 water system that supplies every house and nearly every farm in the district with water for domestic and irrigation purposes. They have built a $45,000 twenty-two bed hospital. They have a voluntary fire brigade with a $7,500 modern fire engine; in all $10,000 worth of equipment.
I give that as an illustration of the development of a small community. It is in these

Coal
small communities that democracy prevails to a greater extent than in the larger centres. When this unincorporated village decides to take action it is done by getting the board of trade, the women's institute, the farmers' institute and the Canadian Legion representatives together. This is only one illustration of many that I could give of the small towns and communities in my constituency that are not being served under this act by the lending institutions.
In my opinion we should do our level best to further the development of our small communities, and that is not being done under this act. It is in the small communities where the greatest opportunities to build homes and bring up families to the best advantage are to be found.
I support the arrangement for dominion-provincial co-operation in the building of subsidized housing. We are hopeful that this will produce results for industrial workers and those who live in the larger centres. We are hopeful that the opportunities provided under the act to co-operative societies to borrow money for the building of houses will be fruitful. But I want to emphasize that under this act as it is being operated at the present time the small towns, the small villages and the rural communities of Canada are not receiving the service they should. I urge the minister to investigate this situation so that the provisions of this act will be available, not only to those in the larger centres but to those who work in and build up our small towns, small villages and rural communities. I am speaking on behalf of the rural folk who have been denied the service that they should receive under this act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the third time and passed.

that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That It is expedient to present a bill to amend the Veterans Land Act, 1942, for the following among other purposes:
To make the benefits of the act available to veterans in receipt of pensions for disabilities which are not the result of service but were incurred during service; to provide conditions under which modifications may be made at the request of veterans in current and future contracts made thereunder; to provide conditions under which adjustments may be made with veterans who have surrendered their contracts, and for the absorption of past abnormal building costs.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
